title: Kerala Crash Kills NRI Family of Three; 36-Hour Arrest Delay Raises Questions
excerpt: The deaths of Gulf returnee Muneer, his wife and their 3-year-old son have revived questions about delayed alcohol evidence — echoing the 2019 Venkitaraman case.
body:
• Muneer, a 35-year-old Gulf returnee from Thrissur, his 25-year-old wife Shafna and their 3-year-old son were killed when a car rammed their motorcycle on the Kunnamkulam–Guruvayur road late on September 5.
  • The accused driver, 31-year-old Ben of Arthat, allegedly fled the scene and surrendered to police roughly 36 hours later, on September 7.
  • The delay has raised questions about whether crucial alcohol evidence was compromised — blood-alcohol levels fall over time — echoing the 2019 Sriram Venkitaraman hit-and-run case.
  • Police say they actively hunted the absconding driver, issuing a lookout notice on September 6, and maintain the blood test is not their only evidence.

A car crash in Kerala's Thrissur district has killed an NRI family of three and revived the same questions that followed the 2019 hit-and-run case involving IAS officer Sriram Venkitaraman: whether a delay of about 36 hours fatally weakened the drunk-driving evidence.

Muneer, a 35-year-old Gulf returnee, his wife Shafna, 25, and their 3-year-old son Muhammad Ameen Ibac died after the motorcycle they were riding was rammed by a car at Kurukkanpara, near Arthat, on the Kunnamkulam–Guruvayur road at about 11:38 pm on Friday, September 5. The family, from Panchavadi Thazhatheth House at Edakkazhiyur in Chavakkad, was returning home after attending a wedding. Muneer had stopped the motorcycle by the roadside to take a phone call when the car, travelling from Kunnamkulam toward Guruvayur, struck it. All three were thrown from the motorcycle and taken to hospital; none survived.

The 36-hour gap

Police allege the car was driven by 31-year-old Ben of Arthat, who they say was speeding and under the influence of alcohol, and who fled the scene without arranging medical help or informing authorities. He did not surrender until September 7, when he walked into the Kunnamkulam police station — roughly 36 hours after the crash — and was arrested.

Police say they spent those hours hunting him: a lookout notice was issued on September 6, several locations were searched, his residence was monitored, and airports, railway stations and checkpoints across the state were alerted. Two passengers from the car were taken in for questioning the night of the crash, and three other occupants — Ajith, Shijil and Danish — were arrested on September 8.

The concern, voiced in the reporting and by legal experts, is evidentiary. Ben underwent a medical examination after his arrest and his blood sample was sent to the Regional Chemical Laboratory in Kakkanad — but blood-alcohol levels fall with every passing hour. As Pravasi Samwad's report noted, legal experts stress that suspected drunk-driving cases require prompt medical examination. With the alcohol test compromised by the delay, investigators are relying on CCTV footage, eyewitness accounts and forensic findings.

The Venkitaraman parallel

The case has revived memories of the August 3, 2019 death of journalist K.M. Basheer, bureau chief of the Malayalam newspaper Siraj, in Thiruvananthapuram. IAS officer Sriram Venkitaraman was arrested about 17 hours later, charged with rash driving and culpable homicide not amounting to murder, amid allegations he had been driving in an inebriated state. In that case, the delay was in collecting his blood sample after he was already in custody — he had checked himself out of the government hospital where police took him — and the Kerala High Court later pulled up the police for not collecting blood samples and fingerprints immediately.

The facts differ — in the Kunnamkulam case the delay was in arresting an absconding driver, not in testing one in custody — but the shared thread is the same: in a fatal suspected-drunk-driving crash, the timely collection of alcohol evidence was undermined, and with it, public confidence in the investigation.

Police push back

Investigating officer Rohit Chevayur has pushed back against the suggestion that the delay guts the case, saying the blood test is not the only evidence being considered. Police maintain they took sustained steps to locate the accused after he went absconding. No independent probe into the handling of the delay has been reported, and no statements from the victims' family have appeared in the coverage so far.

Diaspora angle

Muneer was a Gulf returnee — one of the millions of Keralites whose years in the Gulf build the houses and futures their families live in. His death, alongside his wife and young son, has landed heavily in a state where every neighbourhood has a family with someone working abroad. For the diaspora, the case is another reminder that the road-safety crisis waiting back home does not spare anyone.

What's next

The chemical laboratory's analysis of Ben's blood sample is awaited, alongside the forensic and CCTV evidence. Whether the case holds without a timely alcohol test will be the measure of the investigation — and of whether the lessons of 2019 were learned.
